lesson.title: Reviewer Methodology Framework
lesson.summary: Teach reviewers how to think before any domain-specific reasoning begins.
learningObjectives: Prioritize strong evidence over weak evidence.
Use context, exceptions, and confidence correctly.
Avoid false positives and false negatives.
Recognize when more context is required.

reviewerQuestions.reasoningGuidance: Start with a neutral observation before any finding.
evidenceRequirements: The answer must cite literal evidence.

reviewerQuestions.reasoningGuidance: Name the strongest evidence, not every clue.
evidenceRequirements: The answer must identify the strongest local support.

reviewerQuestions.reasoningGuidance: Track nearby sentences and cross-scene context.
evidenceRequirements: The answer must use scene or story context.

reviewerQuestions.purpose: Does another sentence change the meaning?
reviewerQuestions.reasoningGuidance: Never stop at one sentence when more context exists.
evidenceRequirements: The answer must mention the relevant sentence pair.

reviewerQuestions.purpose: Does another scene change the meaning?
evidenceRequirements: The answer must cite the scene link.

reviewerQuestions.reasoningGuidance: Separate review comment, possible finding, and confirmed finding.
evidenceRequirements: The answer must not overstate certainty.

reviewerQuestions.reasoningGuidance: Calibrate confidence to the quality of the evidence.
evidenceRequirements: The answer must reflect evidence strength.

reviewerQuestions.reasoningGuidance: Check quotation, fiction, history, education, and other exceptions.
evidenceRequirements: The answer must reference the exception cue.

reviewerQuestions.purpose: Could this be a false positive?
evidenceRequirements: The answer must explain the false positive risk.

reviewerQuestions.reasoningGuidance: Look for undercalled evidence or hidden context.
evidenceRequirements: The answer must explain the false negative risk.

examples: A reviewer first notes an observation, then decides whether the evidence is enough for a finding.
A later scene can lower or raise confidence.
An exception like quotation or fiction can prevent an overread conclusion.
counterExamples: Turning every observation into a confirmed finding.

minimum: At least one literal clue must be present in the local chunk.
The reviewer must identify the relevant speaker, target, or context cue when available.
strong: Multiple independent cues point to the same interpretation.
The local chunk and surrounding context reinforce each other.
A later sentence or scene confirms the initial reading.
weak: Only one sentence supports the interpretation.
The scene is ambiguous or partially hidden.
insufficient: Inventing a relationship or intent not supported by the text.
confidenceGuidance: High confidence when evidence is direct and corroborated.
Medium confidence when evidence is plausible but incomplete.
Low confidence when evidence is weak or contradictory.
Review required when the scene is ambiguous or exception-prone.
